query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the high configurational entropy accelerates the selective diffusion and surface segregation of passivating elements (particularly aluminum), which promotes the rapid formation and long-term retention of a coherent, protective Al2O3 oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloy (e.g., a baseline composition similar to CrMnFeCoNi) with controlled variations in aluminum content.
generation.intervention: Prepare two HEA variants: one with a baseline (lower) Al content and one with an enhanced Al content. Subject both to high-temperature oxidation in air using in situ, time-resolved techniques (e.g., high-temperature X-ray diffraction coupled with spatially resolved elemental analysis).
generation.conditions: Oxidation experiments conducted in air at temperatures above 800°C (e.g., 850–1100°C), replicating high-temperature service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and retention of an Al2O3-dominated oxide scale, enabled by selective aluminum segregation from the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the alloy facilitates accelerated diffusion and preferential segregation of aluminum to the surface. This results in the formation of a self-healing, densely adherent Al2O3 layer that acts as an effective oxidation barrier, contrasting with the formation of less protective, mixed oxides in low-Al HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA with enhanced Al content will show rapid development of a uniform, dense, and coherent Al2O3 layer with reduced overall oxidation rates, compared to the baseline low-Al alloy which is predicted to form mixed or non-coherent oxide scales and exhibit higher oxidation kinetics.
generation.baseline: A comparable HEA composition with lower Al content, which under similar high-temperature conditions forms non-protective or mixed oxide scales and displays higher oxidation penetration.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply under high-temperature oxidation conditions in oxidizing atmospheres (air) above approximately 800°C; effects may be different in non-oxidizing atmospheres or at lower temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of Al content needed to shift the oxidation behavior, and the quantitative differences in diffusion rates and oxide scale properties, require further investigation using in situ techniques.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with baseline (lower) and one with enhanced aluminum content. Heat both sets in air at 850°C using an in situ characterization setup combining high-temperature XRD and spatially resolved EDS to monitor real-time oxide formation and diffusion profiles over time.
measurements: Oxide scale composition and phase identification (with emphasis on Al2O3 presence and continuity)
Time-resolved measurements of elemental segregation (especially Al) at the oxide/alloy interface
Oxide scale thickness and integrity over the oxidation duration
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced-Al alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the rate or extent of Al surface segregation and no corresponding improvement in the formation of a coherent, protective Al2O3 oxide layer is observed relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 presents line scanning energy spectrum diagrams of the cross section of the AlTiNiCuCo1.0 alloy oxide layer after oxidation for 50 and 100 h at 800 °C. After 100 h oxidation, the oxide film was thicker than that after 50 h, but the change in thickness was not apparent. This indicates that the oxide film of an HEA of this composition under high-temperature oxidation is relatively dense and plays a certain protective role for the alloy; thus, the alloy has better high-temperature oxidation resistance. It can be seen from Figure 8a, representing 50 h oxidation, that the oxide layer still contained large amounts of Al, Ti, and O elements. It was presumed that there were mainly two oxides, Al2O3 and TiO2, in the oxide layer. After oxidation for 100 h, the contents of Al and Ti in the oxide layer were greater, and the content of Co was significantly increased. Combining this with XRD analysis results, it was found that there were three oxides present: CoAl2O4, Al2O3, and TiO2.

At 800 °C, AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) series HEAs have certain high-temperature oxidation resistance and conform to the Δm=K1tn (n = 1) oxidation mode. The oxidation resistance of the AlTiNiCuCox series HEAs at high temperature is closely related to the Co content. With increasing oxidation time, the overall oxide content in the alloys increases, and the high-temperature oxidation resistance becomes progressively worse. With increasing Co content, a transition layer gradually appears. Among the alloys, the oxide films of AlTiNiCuCo1.0 oxidized for 50 and 100 h were thinner; AlTiNiCuCo1.0 has higher oxidation resistance at high temperature compared to alloys with other amounts of Co that were tested. In the process of high-temperature oxidation of AlTiNiCuCox series HEAs, the interface reaction initially dominates, and metal elements and oxygen in the alloy react to form ions as a result of direct contact; then, ions diffuse and are transported in the oxide film, and the diffusion process gradually becomes the dominant oxidation factor. frame.system: High-entropy alloys composed of multiple principal elements in a single-phase, homogeneous microstructure prior to oxidation.
frame.goal: To mechanistically explain how these alloys develop and retain a protective oxide layer under high-temperature conditions, thereby providing enhanced oxidation resistance.
frame.limitation: The precise mechanism by which the complex, high-entropy compositions lead to the formation, adhesion, and long-term stability of the protective oxide scale is not well understood.

decision.trend: Early studies in high-temperature oxidation of high-entropy alloys first focused on documenting the oxidation kinetics and oxide scale structures in refractory HEAs (e.g., PMC6317005, 2018). These investigations identified mixed oxide scales and temperature‐dependent kinetics, hinting at a role for key elements (like Al and Cr) in forming the protective layer. Subsequent longer-duration experiments (PMC6513993, 2019) revealed that specific oxide phases (e.g., CrTaO4-based) can develop to impart oxidation resistance. More recently, in situ techniques (PMC10384371, 2023) have provided dynamic, thermodynamic insight into phase evolution during oxidation, and advanced coating methods (PMC10856430, 2024) have been used to examine the initial layered oxide formation. Throughout, the work has progressively moved from macroscopic kinetic studies toward detailed phase identification and real-time monitoring of element segregation.
decision.unsolved: Despite the documentation of oxide scale formation and phase evolution, the direct mechanistic link between high configurational entropy and the formation and long-term retention of the protective oxide layer remains unclear. In particular, it is not known whether accelerated or selective elemental diffusion—mediated by the high entropy—drives the formation of a stable, self-healing Al-rich (or other element–rich) oxide barrier under high-temperature conditions, and how this differs from conventional alloys.
decision.lever: Implementing time-resolved, element-specific in situ characterization (for example, combining high-temperature X-ray diffraction with spatially resolved EDS or in situ atom probe tomography) on HEAs with controlled variations in Al content to directly monitor the kinetics and spatial distribution of key elements during oxidation.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that the high configurational entropy in the alloy accelerates selective diffusion and segregation (especially of Al or other reactive elements) to form a robust, self-adherent protective oxide layer. It builds on the trend of using in situ techniques to capture dynamic phase formation and offers a controlled comparison by tuning the elemental activity relative to a baseline alloy, fulfilling the experimental constraints and mechanistic cues outlined in the research question.
